e.t: This Hebrew word is the personal name “Balak.” It identifies a particular person in the Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name occurs 43 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, beginning in Numbers 22:2 and continuing through Micah 6:5. Most occurrences are in Numbers 22, where the name appears repeatedly in speech and reported events. Its precise significance in any individual verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its ordinary lexical function is simply to name Balak.

This word refers to Baal Meon, a place-name in the Old Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than as an ordinary description or action. The name appears six times in three Old Testament verses, from Numbers through Ezekiel, and English renderings preserve it as “Baal” and “Meon.” Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic role is to identify the location called Baal Meon.

The Hebrew word means “clean.” It functions as a describing word, identifying a person or thing as clean rather than expressing an action. In its seven Old Testament occurrences, it carries this central sense. The word points to a condition of cleanness within its sentence, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force. It can therefore describe the stated condition of whatever person or thing the verse places under consideration.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “redemption.” As a noun, it identifies redemption as a matter, act, or provision rather than describing an action by itself. It occurs 14 times in the Old Testament, with several occurrences in Leviticus 25 and others in Jeremiah, Ruth, and Ezekiel. The word can therefore name redemption as a recognized provision or transaction within Israel’s life, while the surrounding passage determines its precise application in each occurrence.

Adoniram is a personal name, referring to a man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both times in 1 Kings: 4:6 and 5:14. Since it functions as a proper name, its ordinary meaning is the identification of this individual, and its precise role in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. The English rendering is consistently “Adoniram.”

This Hebrew word describes joyful gladness—an intense sense of rejoicing or delight. It can also express something done “exceedingly,” showing that the word may emphasize the strength of the joy involved. It occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including poetic passages and descriptions of celebration. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea is strong, outwardly expressed joy rather than mere quiet satisfaction.

This Hebrew word means “like,” expressing comparison or resemblance between one thing and another. It functions as a comparison word rather than naming an object, person, or action. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Psalm 17:12. Its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic role is to indicate likeness: something is being presented as resembling or being comparable to something else.

Dophkah is the name of a place in the Israelites’ wilderness journey. As a proper name, it identifies a location rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Numbers 33, at Numbers 33:12 and 33:13. The available usage preserves it as “Dophkah,” so its precise name meaning is not established here; its clear function is to identify a place in the journey record.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “wickedness,” referring to conduct that is morally evil and seriously wrong. It is used across the Old Testament for sinful acts and behavior condemned by God, including personal wrongdoing and corrupt conduct. The word occurs 29 times in 27 Hebrew Old Testament verses, showing that it describes a recurring category of serious evil rather than one isolated act. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

“Rechabites” is the name of a particular people or family group mentioned in the Hebrew Old Testament. It functions as a proper designation rather than a general description of a person, action, or quality. This Hebrew word occurs once in the Old Testament corpus, at Jeremiah 35:3. The name identifies the group in that passage, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain its specific role there.

This Hebrew word refers to “clefts”—narrow openings or fissures in rock or a mountain. It names a physical place rather than an action or quality. The word occurs three times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, and each occurrence is rendered “clefts.” Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its ordinary meaning is a cleft or crevice that can be found among rocky places.

This Hebrew word is the personal name “Haziel,” identifying one individual rather than describing an action or quality. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 23:9, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Haziel.” Its use here supports understanding it as a proper name, but the supplied material does not establish an additional lexical meaning or explain the person’s role in that verse.

e.t: “Hiel” is a personal name, identifying a particular man rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Kings 16:34, so its ordinary function is to identify that individual in the biblical narrative. The name itself should therefore be read as a person’s designation, while the surrounding verse supplies the details about him and what he did. Its rendering remains “Hiel” in the English translations represented here.

Its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears, but its central sense remains connected with what is pleasant.

It is used as something associated with people or places, and the surrounding SEE relationships present it as something connected with, or given to, others. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Ezekiel, across eight verses. Its repeated use in Ezekiel 32 shows the word’s consistent connection with terror rather than a broad range of unrelated meanings.

The surrounding SEE pattern identifies the name with birth or begetting relationships, showing that Jehoaddah is presented as a person within a family line. The available passage evidence does not provide a broader ordinary meaning beyond this name’s identification of that individual.

e.t: Ahasuerus is a proper name referring to a king. It is not a general word describing an action, quality, or object, but the personal designation used for this ruler. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 32 times in 30 verses, chiefly in Esther, with additional occurrences in Ezra and Daniel. The name appears in passages describing the king’s rule, speech, decisions, and commands. Its precise significance in any particular verse comes from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the name Ahasuerus.

This Hebrew verb means “possess.” It describes taking or holding something as one’s possession, especially land or an inheritance. In the Old Testament, it is frequently used when God gives Israel a land to possess, and it can also describe dispossessing people so that another may take their place. The word occurs 232 times in the Hebrew Bible, showing that possession is a broad and recurring idea in its scriptural use.

Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but the available usage supports the simple sense of “son” rather than a broader set of meanings.

e.t: Chelubai is a personal name, rendered “Chelubai.” It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 2:9. The word identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. Its recorded use is connected with a genealogy and a birth or begetting relationship, so its function there is to identify a person within a family record. No broader ordinary meaning is established by this single occurrence.

e.t: This Hebrew word describes something “fruitful,” especially in connection with agricultural abundance. It can refer to the fertility or productivity associated with cultivated land and its produce, whether in worship offerings, harvest observance, or descriptions of a prosperous region. The word occurs 16 times in the Old Testament, so its basic sense is broader than a single kind of crop: it points to flourishing agricultural provision. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “was.” It functions as a verb, helping state that someone or something was in a particular condition. In its two Old Testament occurrences, it appears once in Genesis and once in Proverbs, making its recorded use uncommon in the Hebrew corpus. The surrounding words determine the specific condition being stated in each passage; the basic contribution of the word is to express that state as something that was.

This Hebrew word refers to “Lecah,” functioning as a personal or place name rather than describing an action, quality, or object in general. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at 1 Chronicles 4:21, and the available English renderings preserve it as “Lecah.” The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the exact identity associated with the name must be determined from that passage. Its central meaning is therefore the proper name itself: Lecah.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “food”—what people eat for nourishment. It can describe provisions gathered, stored, bought, distributed, or prepared for a meal. In its Old Testament usage, the word commonly functions as the object of actions involving food, such as giving it, purchasing it, measuring it, or eating it. It occurs 44 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a broad everyday use for physical sustenance rather than a specialized term.

This Hebrew word refers to “deceits,” naming things that mislead rather than express what is true. It functions as a noun for deceptive matters, not as an action or command. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 30:10. Its basic sense remains focused on deceit itself; the surrounding verse determines the specific force intended in that occurrence.

The name occurs 19 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with most occurrences in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles and two in Jeremiah. Its precise significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding narrative, but its basic function is simply to name the individual Micaiah.

The word can also be used in statements about God’s relationship to such a place, but its central sense remains a den or animal dwelling place.

e.t: Eliashib is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It appears 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, especially in Nehemiah, and is consistently rendered “Eliashib.” The name occurs in genealogical material and in passages involving people connected with the community of Israel. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on which person named Eliashib is being mentioned.

This Hebrew word refers to something “bitter,” especially “herbs” with a sharp or unpleasant taste. In the Old Testament, it occurs three times: twice in instructions concerning the Passover meal and once in Lamentations. Its central idea is bitterness, whether describing a food eaten with the meal or the figurative experience of distress. The surrounding passage determines whether the word points to bitter plants as food or to bitterness as a felt condition.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “gifts”—things given to another person. Its recorded use presents it as the object of giving, so the word focuses on what is handed over rather than on the giver or recipient. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Ezekiel 16:33. Its associated scriptural pattern is giving, reinforcing the sense of gifts offered or transferred to someone else.

This Hebrew word describes acting deceptively against someone, including plotting or dealing falsely. It can be rendered “conspired” when the emphasis is on a planned action and “deceiver” when the emphasis is on the person or conduct involved. In the Old Testament, it occurs four times, each in a different verse, and functions as a term for deliberate deceit rather than ordinary error or misunderstanding. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding wording.

This Hebrew word refers to a “leopard,” the name of an animal. It functions as a direct animal term, not as a description of an action or quality. In the Hebrew corpus represented here, it appears once, in Daniel 7:6. The word therefore carries a narrow, concrete meaning rather than a broad abstract idea. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word refers to “merchandise,” meaning items involved in trade or exchange. It functions as a noun describing something bought, sold, or transported for commercial purposes. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ezekiel 27:15. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s exact role in that sentence must be understood from its immediate context, but its basic meaning points to commercial goods or trade property.

Its normal sense remains focused on the whirlwind itself; the surrounding verse determines what role that whirlwind has in a particular passage.

In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs seven times, and its usual English rendering is “cakes.” The word’s basic sense remains consistent across its uses, while the surrounding passage determines how the cake is being prepared, presented, or eaten in a particular verse.

Adiel is a personal name, rendered “Adiel.” It identifies people mentioned in the Old Testament, rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles: 1 Chronicles 4:36, 9:12, and 27:25. Since no explicit definition or description of the name is provided here, its supported meaning is its function as an individual’s name. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain which Adiel is intended in any particular passage.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “handful,” referring to an amount that can be held in one hand. It is used four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in Jeremiah, Amos, Micah, and Zechariah. Its occurrences describe a measurable quantity rather than an action or quality. The surrounding wording determines what is being gathered, held, or compared, but the word itself points to the quantity of a handful.

This Hebrew word means “poor,” describing a person with little material wealth or resources. It occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Daniel 4:27, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse rather than repeated biblical usage. As a descriptive word, it identifies a person’s low economic condition. The available English renderings consistently use “poor,” supporting this central meaning without establishing additional meanings.

“Interpreting” refers to the act of making something understood by stating its meaning. This Hebrew word functions as an action word rather than a name or description of a person or thing.
